note: Health and medical breakthroughs that were in the news in January 2024, in date order, then three items from this week (Nov 12 to 19, 2026) as the closer. (AI) at the end of a title marks a breakthrough where AI was part of the work.

topics.title: World's first partial heart transplant: the valves grow with the baby
topics.why_now: On January 2, 2024, Duke surgeons published the first results of a partial heart transplant in JAMA. The baby, Owen Monroe, got it at 17 days old in 2022, and the transplanted valves were growing along with him.
topics.angle: A brand new kind of surgery that could mean fewer repeat operations for kids, and more donor hearts put to use. The pace of medical firsts is picking up across the board.

tabs.label: Deseret News: first partial heart transplant hailed as success
highlights: The hearts and valves transplanted into an infant in 2022 are growing along with the child
requires only about a fourth as much medicine to suppress the immune system

facts.text: Owen Monroe was 17 days old in the spring of 2022 when he became the first to receive a partial heart transplant.
A partial heart transplant requires only about a fourth as much immune-suppressing medicine as a full transplant, per the article.
Duke's chief of pediatric cardiac surgery, Dr. Joseph Turek, said the approach could potentially double the number of hearts used for children with heart disease.

prompts: Imagine being the first human ever to get this. Seventeen days old. And the valves are growing with him.
Turek says this could double the number of donor hearts that help kids. That is the kind of multiplier I love.

tabs.label: JAMA (via Duke Scholars): the case report
highlights: To deliver the first heart valve implant that grows.

facts.text: The paper, 'Partial Heart Transplant in a Neonate With Irreparable Truncal Valve Dysfunction', ran in JAMA on January 2, 2024, by Joseph W. Turek and colleagues.
The abstract reports that echocardiography showed adaptive growth and excellent function of the transplanted valves.

careful: This January 2024 paper is a single-patient case report (the title says 'in a Neonate'). Say 'the first patient', not 'a trial'.
prompts: This is published in JAMA. Not a press stunt, a real paper. One kid so far, but a door just opened.

topics.title: A whole new class of antibiotic against a hospital superbug
topics.why_now: On January 3, 2024, Roche and Harvard scientists published a pair of Nature papers on zosurabalpin, a new type of antibiotic that kills drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) in lab and mouse tests.
topics.angle: Superbugs are one of the scariest long-term costs in medicine. A new antibiotic class after decades of nothing is the kind of progress that saves hospitals, money and lives.

tabs.label: Freethink: superbug-killing antibiotic now in human trials
highlights: it could lead to an entirely new class of antibiotics

facts.text: Scientists from Roche and Harvard University described the new antibiotic, zosurabalpin, in a pair of papers in Nature.
Zosurabalpin proved safe and tolerable in two completed phase 1 trials involving a total of 64 people, per the article.
The article says it could become the first new antibiotic approved against gram-negative bacteria in more than 50 years, and that CRAB is one of WHO's top three priority pathogens.

careful: In January 2024 this was early phase 1, not an approved drug. Its 2026 status was not checked here, so say 'was in early human trials at the time'.
prompts: More than 50 years without a new antibiotic for this whole bug family. Then boom, a new class, in Nature.
Drug-resistant infections cost hospitals a fortune. Every new weapon here is a win for the whole economy, not just the patient.

tabs.label: Nature: A novel antibiotic class targeting the lipopolysaccharide transporter
highlights: A novel antibiotic class targeting the lipopolysaccharide transporter
zosurabalpin (RG6006)

facts.text: The paper by Claudia Zampaloni and colleagues appeared in Nature (vol. 625), first published January 3, 2024.

The compounds block the LptB2FGC complex that moves lipopolysaccharide to the bacteria's outer membrane, and zosurabalpin worked against resistant clinical isolates in the lab and in mouse infection models.

prompts: It attacks how the bacteria build their outer wall. A totally new way in.

topics.title: Ultrasound opens the blood-brain barrier to clear Alzheimer's plaque faster
topics.why_now: In the first week of January 2024, the New England Journal of Medicine published a small West Virginia University study: focused ultrasound briefly opened the blood-brain barrier while patients got an anti-amyloid drug, and plaque dropped more on the treated side.
topics.angle: The brain has always been the hardest place to get a drug into. Cracking that open, even in three people, points at a future where brain disease gets the same speed-up the rest of medicine is getting.

tabs.label: Physics World: focused ultrasound plus plaque-reducing drugs
highlights: small first-in-human clinical trial

facts.text: The proof-of-concept trial at West Virginia University's Rockefeller Neuroscience Institute included three participants with mild Alzheimer's disease, and early results appeared in NEJM.
At 26 weeks, plaque in the ultrasound-treated brain areas averaged 32% lower than in the matching untreated areas on the other side.

careful: Three patients, no placebo group: the 32% compares one side of each brain with the other. The NEJM editorial said additional studies are needed for long-term safety and efficacy.
prompts: The blood-brain barrier is like a bouncer. This is sound waves getting the drug past the bouncer, for a few hours, on purpose.
Three patients. Tiny. But this is how every big thing starts, and the pace of these first-in-human studies keeps climbing.

tabs.label: NEJM: Ultrasound Blood-Brain Barrier Opening and Aducanumab in Alzheimer's Disease
highlights: numerically greater

facts.text: The NEJM paper, first author Ali R. Rezai, applied focused ultrasound with each of six monthly aducanumab infusions to temporarily open the blood-brain barrier in three people with Alzheimer's disease.
Biogen announced on January 31, 2024 that it was walking away from aducanumab, saying the decision was not based on efficacy or safety concerns.

careful: The drug used here (aducanumab, Aduhelm) was dropped by Biogen at the end of the same month. Frame the win as the ultrasound delivery method, not the drug.
prompts: The drug they used got shelved, but the delivery trick is the real story. Plug in a better drug and you get the payoff.

topics.title: AI reads eye photos and predicts diabetic eye disease years ahead (AI)
topics.ai_how: A deep learning model (DeepDR Plus) reads retinal photos and predicts when diabetic retinopathy will get worse, up to five years out.
topics.why_now: On January 4, 2024, Nature Medicine published DeepDR Plus, a deep learning system from China trained on hundreds of thousands of eye photos that predicts the time until diabetic eye disease progresses.
topics.angle: This is AI making the health system cheaper: fewer unneeded screening visits for low-risk people, attention focused on the ones who need it. Same care, less cost, and that adds up across millions of diabetics.

tabs.label: News-Medical: Can AI predict diabetic eye disease progression?
highlights: the average screening interval could be prolonged from 12 months to 31.97 months

facts.text: The system could predict the risk of and time to diabetic retinopathy progression within five years, using photos of the eye.
It was pre-trained on over 700,000 fundus images from roughly 179,000 people with diabetes in Shanghai.

careful: The authors note it was trained on a Chinese population and has not been tested in actual clinical use. The longer screening gap is a modeled estimate, not a proven outcome.
prompts: Right now diabetics get told to screen every year. This AI says, for a lot of you, every two and a half years is fine. That is real money saved.
AI is not replacing the eye doctor here. It is telling the system where to spend the eye doctor's time.

tabs.label: Nature Medicine (PMC): A deep learning system for predicting time to progression of diabetic retinopathy
highlights: extend the mean screening interval from 12 months to 31.97 months

facts.text: Published in Nature Medicine on January 4, 2024; pretraining used 717,308 images from 179,327 participants with diabetes.

prompts: Seven hundred thousand eye photos. No human could ever look at that many. That is the whole point of AI in medicine.

topics.title: FDA approves the first molluscum gel families can apply at home
topics.why_now: On January 5, 2024, the FDA approved Zelsuvmi (berdazimer), a nitric-oxide-releasing gel for molluscum contagiosum, the only novel drug the FDA approved that month.
topics.angle: Not every breakthrough is flashy. Moving a treatment from the clinic to the kitchen table saves families time and the system money, and that is progress too.

tabs.label: Practical Dermatology: FDA approves Zelsuvmi as first-in-class
highlights: can be applied by patients, parents, or caregivers at home

facts.text: Zelsuvmi is a nitric oxide releasing agent, approved for adults and children one year of age and older.
The B-SIMPLE Phase 3 program enrolled 1,598 patients.

careful: Keep the 'first' to 'first gel families can apply at home'. Another molluscum treatment may already have been approved in 2023, so do not call it the first treatment ever.
prompts: Small one, but I like it: a kid's skin infection you can now treat at home instead of a doctor's office.

tabs.label: FDA: Novel Drug Approvals for 2024
highlights: To treat molluscum contagiosum

facts.text: The FDA list shows Zelsuvmi (berdazimer) approved 1/5/2024 to treat molluscum contagiosum, the only novel drug approval dated January 2024 on the list.

prompts: This is the official FDA list for 2024. January had one new drug on it, and this is it.

topics.title: Google's AMIE chatbot matches doctors in diagnostic conversations (AI)
topics.ai_how: AMIE is a large language model trained to take a patient history and suggest diagnoses in a text chat.
topics.why_now: On January 11, 2024, Google posted a preprint on AMIE, an AI system for diagnostic conversations. In simulated text consultations with patient actors, it scored better than primary care doctors on most measures.
topics.angle: Access to a good doctor is one of the scarcest things on earth. An AI that can take a solid history first means more people get seen, faster, for less. That is a productivity jump for the whole health system.

tabs.label: pharmaphorum: Google chatbot tops docs on accuracy, bedside manner
highlights: remains experimental and is in no way ready to replace the usual patient-doctor interaction

facts.text: The study covered 149 healthcare scenarios in text-based consultations with patient actors, and neither side knew whether they were talking to an AI or a doctor.
Specialists rated AMIE better on 28 of 32 measures, and conversation quality was rated better on 24 of 26 measures.

careful: January 2024 was a preprint with actors, not real patients, and doctors used an unfamiliar text-chat format. Say 'in a simulated test'.
prompts: Patient actors rated the AI better on bedside manner. The AI. Better bedside manner. Let that sink in.
This is the one that makes my whole point: AI is going to make good medical advice cheap and everywhere.

tabs.label: arXiv: Towards Conversational Diagnostic AI
highlights: superior performance on 28 of 32 axes according to specialist physicians

facts.text: Submitted to arXiv on 11 January 2024; AMIE was compared with 20 primary care physicians across 149 case scenarios from Canada, the UK and India.

In October 2026, Google and Beth Israel Deaconess published a real-world AMIE study in The Lancet: 98 patients chatted with it before urgent care visits, and its differential diagnoses matched the doctors' final diagnoses 90% of the time.

careful: The 2026 Lancet study was 98 patients at one clinic, and the authors say larger trials are needed.
prompts: January 2024, a preprint. By October 2026, a real clinic, real patients, The Lancet. That is how fast this is moving.

topics.title: CRISPR therapy Casgevy approved for beta thalassemia
topics.why_now: On January 16, 2024, the FDA approved Casgevy, the CRISPR gene-edited therapy from Vertex and CRISPR Therapeutics, for transfusion-dependent beta thalassemia in patients 12 and older, its second approval after sickle cell disease in December 2023.
topics.angle: Gene editing went from a lab tool to an approved one-time treatment in around a decade. A patient who needed blood transfusions for life is a huge lifetime cost; a one-time fix changes the math for families and for the system.

tabs.label: Managed Healthcare Executive: FDA approves second indication for Casgevy
highlights: wholesale acquisition cost of $2.2 million

facts.text: The FDA approved Casgevy for transfusion-dependent beta thalassemia in patients 12 years and older; it was first approved for sickle cell disease in early December 2023.
Casgevy has a wholesale acquisition cost of $2.2 million.

careful: This is the second Casgevy approval, not the first CRISPR approval (that was sickle cell, December 8, 2023).
prompts: Two point two million dollars sounds insane, until you compare it to a lifetime of transfusions.
One and done. You edit the patient's own cells once. That is a new business model for medicine.

tabs.label: CRISPR Therapeutics 8-K (SEC): the approval
highlights: On January 16, 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved CASGEVY

facts.text: CRISPR Therapeutics' filing states the FDA approved Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), a CRISPR/Cas9 gene-edited cell therapy, on January 16, 2024, for transfusion-dependent beta thalassemia in patients 12 and older.
The FDA called Casgevy the first FDA-approved therapy utilizing CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing when it approved it for sickle cell disease on December 8, 2023.

prompts: Two diseases in six weeks for the same CRISPR therapy. The approvals are stacking up.

topics.title: FDA clears a handheld AI skin cancer checker for family doctors (AI)
topics.ai_how: An AI algorithm reads light-scattering readings from a skin lesion and gives the doctor an instant result on whether to refer it.
topics.why_now: On January 17, 2024, DermaSensor announced FDA clearance for its handheld device that uses AI-powered spectroscopy to check a lesion for melanoma, basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma, aimed at primary care doctors.
topics.angle: This takes a specialist skill and puts it in a regular doctor's hand. That is the AI economy story in one gadget: specialist-level checks at primary care cost, and more cancers caught early.

tabs.label: pharmaphorum: FDA clears AI skin cancer detection device
highlights: the first FDA-cleared skin cancer device for primary care use

facts.text: The algorithm was developed and trained on more than 20,000 scans of around 4,000 benign and malignant skin lesions.
In a supporting study of 108 primary care physicians, the device cut missed skin cancers by half, from 18% to 9%.

careful: Say 'cleared', not 'approved' (a lower-risk device pathway). Specificity in the pivotal study was low, 20.7%, which can mean extra referrals, per a write-up on DermaSensor's own site: https://www.dermasensor.com/learnings-from-the-first-ai-enabled-skin-cancer-device/
prompts: Missed skin cancers cut in half, in the hands of a regular family doctor. That is AI paying for itself.
Most people never see a dermatologist. This brings the dermatologist's eye to the GP.

tabs.label: DermaSensor press release (BioSpace)
highlights: led by the Mayo Clinic across 22 study centers

facts.text: In the FDA pivotal study, which enrolled over 1,000 patients and was led by the Mayo Clinic across 22 centers, the device had a sensitivity of 96 percent across all 224 skin cancers.

careful: The pivotal trial was 97.1% White, and the FDA required post-market testing in underrepresented populations (same DermaSensor-site write-up).
prompts: Ninety-six percent of the cancers flagged, in the study. Wireless, handheld, instant answer.

topics.title: A simple blood test spots Alzheimer's as well as a spinal tap
topics.why_now: On January 22, 2024, JAMA Neurology published a study of 786 people showing a blood test for the protein p-tau217 identified Alzheimer's brain changes with accuracy comparable to spinal fluid tests.
topics.angle: PET scans and spinal taps are expensive and hard to get. A blood draw that does the same job is a massive cost drop, and it means people find out early enough to plan. Medicine is getting cheaper and faster at the same time.

tabs.label: Alzheimer Europe: blood biomarker test shows strong diagnostic accuracy
highlights: The pTau217 tests proved highly accurate
comparable accuracy to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers

facts.text: The study, published in JAMA Neurology on 22 January 2024, evaluated data from 786 participants across three cohorts.
The article says blood tests may be viable alternatives to more invasive lumbar punctures, noting PET scans and spinal fluid tests are costly and hard to deliver in primary care.

prompts: No needle in your spine, no fancy scan. A blood draw.
Cheaper diagnosis is one of the most underrated ways medicine boosts the economy.

tabs.label: JAMA Neurology: Diagnostic Accuracy of a Plasma p-tau217 Immunoassay
highlights: accurately identified biological AD

facts.text: First author Nicholas J. Ashton; the test's AUC was 0.92 to 0.96 for elevated amyloid and 0.93 to 0.97 for tau pathology, comparable to spinal fluid biomarkers for identifying abnormal PET scans.

careful: AUC is not a plain 'percent correct'. On camera say 'highly accurate, on par with a spinal tap', not '97 percent accurate'.
prompts: On par with a spinal tap, from a blood draw. That is the headline.

topics.title: Cameroon starts the world's first routine malaria vaccine program
topics.why_now: On January 22, 2024, Cameroon added the RTS,S malaria vaccine to its routine childhood shots in 42 high-risk districts, the world's first routine malaria vaccination program.
topics.angle: Malaria has held back whole economies for centuries. Kids who do not get sick go to school, parents keep working. A vaccine moving from trials into routine shots is progress you can measure in GDP.

tabs.label: Global News (Reuters): Cameroon begins malaria vaccine rollout
highlights: first routine vaccine program against the mosquito-borne disease

facts.text: Malaria in Africa kills nearly half a million children under the age of five each year, per the article.
According to Gavi, 19 other countries aimed to roll out the vaccine that year.

careful: This is a rollout milestone, not a new trial result, and the vaccine is not a complete fix on its own. Keep it framed as the first routine program.
prompts: Half a million kids a year in Africa. And now there is a routine shot for it, like measles.

tabs.label: WHO Africa: child health improves one year after the vaccine
highlights: a four-dose protocol in 42 high-malaria-burden health districts

facts.text: WHO says the vaccine was introduced in Cameroon on 22 January 2024, and around 366,000 doses had been given to infants by 31 December 2024.
The 42 districts reported 266,917 malaria cases in 2024, compared with 333,805 in 2023.

careful: The case drop is early health-facility data, not a controlled study. Say 'early data shows fewer cases'.
prompts: One year in, those districts had tens of thousands fewer malaria cases. Early data, but that is the direction you want.

topics.title: Gene therapy lets children born deaf hear
topics.why_now: On January 24, 2024, The Lancet published a trial from Fudan University in China: a one-time gene therapy for otoferlin deafness restored hearing in five of six children. A day earlier, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia announced hearing gains in an 11-year-old boy from Spain.
topics.angle: Kids born deaf, hearing for the first time from one treatment. Gene therapy is moving from one disease to the next faster every year, and each one turns a lifetime cost into a one-time fix.

tabs.label: CBS News (AP): gene therapy helps kids with inherited hearing loss
highlights: an inner ear protein called otoferlin, which helps hair cells transmit sound to the brain

facts.text: The Lancet study found significantly restored hearing in five of six kids treated in China, and the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia reported gains for Aissam Dam of Spain, who was born unable to hear.
The article says 34 million children have deafness or hearing loss.

careful: An expert told AP the children 'don't wind up with perfect hearing'. Say 'hearing restored', never 'cured'.
prompts: A kid who has never heard a sound, hearing for the first time. I mean, come on.
Every gene therapy that works makes the next one faster and cheaper to build. That flywheel is spinning.

tabs.label: The Lancet: AAV1-hOTOF gene therapy for autosomal recessive deafness 9
highlights: Five children had hearing recovery

facts.text: The single-arm trial, published online January 24, 2024, enrolled six children; five had hearing recovery, and no dose-limiting toxicity or serious adverse events occurred.
Harvard Medical School, whose Zheng-Yi Chen was involved, said one of the six showed no improvement and that only six of 425 screened were enrolled.

prompts: Five out of six. One shot into the ear.

topics.title: Neuralink puts its brain chip in its first human patient
topics.why_now: On January 29, 2024, Elon Musk posted that the first human had received a Neuralink implant the day before and was recovering well, the first patient in its PRIME brain-computer interface study.
topics.angle: Paralyzed people controlling a computer with thought. That turns people back into creators and workers, and it is a whole new industry being born. The future is showing up early.

tabs.label: Engadget: Neuralink's brain chip has been implanted in a human
highlights: The first human received an implant from @Neuralink yesterday and is recovering well.
initial results show promising neuron spike detection

facts.text: Musk posted that the first human received an implant from Neuralink the day before and was recovering well, and that initial results showed promising neuron spike detection.
Neuralink began recruiting human patients for its first clinical trial in fall 2023.

careful: In May 2024 Neuralink disclosed that a number of threads retracted from the patient's brain, cutting effective electrodes; it said software changes restored and improved performance. Do not claim it worked perfectly from day one. Source: https://www.theregister.com/2024/05/09/neuralink_trial_update
prompts: Love him or hate him, Musk put a chip in a human brain and the guy went on to play chess with his mind.
Think of what that means for the economy: people who were locked out of work can get back in.

tabs.label: Neuralink blog: first-in-human trial open for recruitment
highlights: control a computer cursor or keyboard using their thoughts alone

facts.text: The PRIME Study runs under an investigational device exemption the FDA granted in May 2023, for people with quadriplegia from cervical spinal cord injury or ALS.
Neuralink later said the first participant used the system for things like playing online chess and Sid Meier's Civilization VI.

careful: Tagged ai 'no' on purpose: Neuralink describes an app that decodes the neural data into cursor movement and does not call it AI. Do not call it an AI breakthrough on camera.
prompts: A robot does the surgery, the chip sits invisible under the skull, and you move a cursor by thinking. Wild.

topics.title: Vertex's non-opioid painkiller passes its Phase 3 tests
topics.why_now: On January 30, 2024, Vertex announced Phase 3 results for VX-548 (suzetrigine), a non-opioid pain pill: it beat placebo after tummy-tuck and bunion surgery, and Vertex planned to file with the FDA by mid-2024.
topics.angle: Opioids have cost the US a staggering amount in lives and money. A strong painkiller that is not an opioid is one of the biggest economic and human wins medicine can deliver, and a year later it was approved.

tabs.label: Patient Care: nonopioid VX-548 reduces post-surgical pain
highlights: investigational selective NaV1.8 inhibitor

facts.text: The trials enrolled adults having abdominoplasty (n = 1118) and bunionectomy (n = 1073), and VX-548 beat placebo on the primary pain endpoint in both.
Median time to meaningful pain relief was 2 hours after abdominoplasty and 4 hours after bunionectomy, versus 8 hours on placebo.
Vertex planned a New Drug Application to the FDA by the middle of 2024.

careful: VX-548 did not beat the hydrocodone/acetaminophen opioid combo, and the opioid combo did better after bunion surgery. Say 'beat placebo', never 'beat opioids'.
prompts: A pain pill that is not an opioid and actually works after surgery. That is the holy grail.
No addiction risk means fewer lives wrecked and fewer billions burned. That is a productivity story too.

tabs.label: FDA (one year later): approves novel non-opioid treatment
highlights: a first-in-class non-opioid analgesic

facts.text: On January 30, 2025, the FDA approved Journavx (suzetrigine) 50 mg tablets for moderate to severe acute pain in adults, calling it the first drug approved in this new class of pain medicines.
The FDA says it reduces pain by targeting a sodium-channel pain pathway in the peripheral nervous system, before pain signals reach the brain.

prompts: January 2024, trial results. January 2025, FDA approved. One year, data to pharmacy.

topics.title: This week: CagriSema lower doses show around 21% weight loss in The Lancet
topics.why_now: On November 14, 2026, Novo Nordisk presented the REDEFINE 9 Phase 3 results at ObesityWeek, published the same day in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology: lower doses of CagriSema gave around 21% average weight loss at 68 weeks.
topics.angle: Obesity drugs keep getting stronger and now work at lower doses. A healthier population is the biggest productivity unlock there is, and this field is moving every few months.

tabs.label: Novo Nordisk: REDEFINE 9 results
highlights: simultaneously published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology

facts.text: REDEFINE 9 was a 68-week Phase 3, placebo-controlled trial in 309 adults with obesity or overweight plus a weight-related complication, without diabetes.

Assuming full adherence, the 1.7 mg and 1.0 mg doses gave estimated average weight loss of 20.7% and 21.0% at 68 weeks, versus 2.0% on placebo; counting everyone regardless of stopping, it was 19.4% and 18.6% versus 4.6%.

careful: CagriSema is still investigational and not approved in the US. The trial was not designed to compare the two doses, and topline numbers may have been released earlier than this week.
prompts: Around 21% body weight, at lower doses than before. These drugs just keep getting better.
Imagine the healthcare bill when a big chunk of obesity-driven disease starts going away.

topics.title: This week: first drug shown to help babies with Niemann-Pick type C live longer
topics.why_now: On November 17, 2026, the FDA approved Lembaz (adrabetadex) from Beren Therapeutics, the first treatment shown to help people with infantile-onset Niemann-Pick disease type C live longer.
topics.angle: Rare diseases used to get nothing. Now they are getting approvals with real survival numbers, and every one of these proves the pipeline is speeding up.

tabs.label: Pharmacy Times: adrabetadex extends survival
highlights: median overall survival of 8.5 years vs 4.9 years in controls

facts.text: Treatment was associated with a 55% reduction in the risk of death, estimated from 36 treated patients compared with a matched external control group.
Beren expects the drug to be available at sites nationwide in early December.

careful: The comparison is against an external control group, not a randomized trial. Lembaz carries a boxed warning for hearing loss, including permanent hearing loss (FDA release).
prompts: Median survival from 4.9 years to 8.5 years. For these families that is everything.

tabs.label: FDA: first drug shown to help infantile-onset NPC patients live longer
highlights: the first treatment shown to help people with a severe form of Niemann-Pick disease type C

facts.text: The FDA says the disease affects an estimated 1 in 150,000 people, and Lembaz is given by a healthcare provider as an injection into the spinal canal every two weeks.

prompts: One in 150,000. Ten years ago nobody would build a drug for that. Now they do.

topics.title: This week: first drug for the brain symptoms of Type 3 Gaucher disease
topics.why_now: On November 18, 2026, the FDA approved Infilbray (venglustat) from Sanofi's Genzyme, a once-daily pill and the first treatment for the neurological symptoms of Type 3 Gaucher disease.
topics.angle: Another 'first' in the same week, and this one is a pill that gets into the brain. Two rare-disease firsts in two days is what an accelerating medical economy looks like.

tabs.label: FDA: first drug to treat neurological symptoms of Type 3 Gaucher
highlights: Infilbray crosses the blood-brain barrier
the first treatment for the neurological symptoms of Type 3 Gaucher disease

facts.text: Infilbray is an oral tablet taken once daily, from Genzyme Corporation, a Sanofi company.
In a randomized, double-blind study of 43 patients aged 12 and older, compared with enzyme replacement therapy, patients on Infilbray showed improvement on a combined measure at Week 52.

prompts: Remember the ultrasound trick from January 2024 to get past the blood-brain barrier? This one is a pill that does it on its own.
Two rare-disease firsts in two days. Tell me medicine is not speeding up.
